title: Lonesome Jim
full_review:
Steve Buscemi, the actor who played Tony Blundetto so memorably on "The Sopranos," is also an accomplished director, as demonstrated in "Lonesome Jim" (IFC), a quirky, slyly humorous, though often languidly paced film.

The titular 27-year-old (Casey Affleck) has been living in New York hoping to make it as a writer, but working as a dog walker and Applebee's waiter. He's in "chronic despair" -- so miserable in the world, he thinks he'd almost rather not be in it -- and has come back to his eccentric homestead of rural Indiana to have a nervous breakdown.

He's greeted effusively by his loving but overly doting mother, Sally (a very endearing Mary Kay Place), who thinks nothing of barging into the bathroom while Jim is in the tub, and speaking to him in gooey terms of endearment (though there's nothing sexual in this).

There's also his father, Don (Seymour Cassel), who takes a back seat to Mom, and glum divorced brother Tim (Kevin Corrigan), who has two small girls.

Jim passively ambles through life, sleeps a lot and eventually goes to work in his parents' factory.

He falls for an attractive nurse, Anika (nice work by Liv Tyler), with whom he commences an affair, and who surprises him, when he comes to her door, with a young son, Ben (Jack Rovello), who accompanies them on their dates.

All of Jim's melancholy talk prompts Tim to run his car into a tree, but the family rallies around Tim after his "accident" while he recovers. Even Anika spends an inordinate amount of time at his bedside, sparking some jealousy on Jim's part, though his suspicions prove unfounded.

Jim is fond of his druggy biker uncle, known as Evil (Mark Boone Junior), who works for Sally and Don. Later, it turns out that Evil has been shipping drugs from the company's FedEx account, and Sally is arrested. (She's such a guilelessly good-natured person, however, that she doesn't even complain, and befriends her jail mates.)

These events -- like almost everything in the film -- are accepted with lackadaisical equanimity, but by the end everything fits.

Buscemi's film (from James C. Strouse's screenplay) is sometimes slow and meandering. Jim is such a laid-back, unmotivated character that it's difficult to summon much interest in his predicament, and the movie's true-to-life candor (a rear view of Jim urinating, for instance) won't appeal to all tastes, but the central protagonist develops as a person, and learns the importance of accepting life for what it is, not what you want it to be.

Jim takes over coaching duties from his incapacitated brother for a young girls' basketball team. Dispirited by their unbroken losing streak, he tells them "You gotta keep playing" and "The past doesn't always predict the future" -- life lessons that pretty much sum up the film's ultimate good message.

The film contains scattered instances of profanity, rough and crude language and expressions, some crass humor, rear and partial nudity, a premarital relationship, sexual banter and lewd images, a prostitute character, a suicide theme and drug references. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
